notes.short: A great statue pictures the kingdoms to come
notes.about: Daniel tells the king his dream: a great statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay, struck on its feet by a stone that becomes a great mountain. Then he explains it: the king is the head of gold, other kingdoms follow, and God will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: The head of the statue was pure gold
figure.means: the king of Babylon and his kingdom, followed by lesser kingdoms in turn, until the kingdom God sets up, pictured by the stone, fills the earth

notes.evidence: Calvin says God represented the four monarchies under this one image, wishing under this figure to show the state of the world until Christ came. Clarke calls the image a political representation of as many governments as it had materials; Albert Barnes, an image well suited to represent successive kingdoms. Matthew Henry says the image represented the kingdoms that would rule in turn.
notes.limit: The dream was a real dream God gave the king; the picture is what it showed, and Daniel explains it in verses 36 to 45. Many read the four parts as Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome.

cites.quote: My assertion is perfectly correct, that interpreters of moderate judgment and candor, all explain the passage of the Babylonian, Persian, Macedonian, and Roman monarchies ... why God represented these four monarchies under this image? ... God therefore wished, under this figure, to represent the future condition of the world till the advent of Christ.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: This image is considered a political representation of as many different governments, as it was composed of materials; and as all these materials are successively inferior to each other, so are the governments in a descending ratio.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The design for which this representation was made to Nebuchadnezzar is clearly unfolded in the explanation which Daniel gives. It may be remarked here, in general, that such an appearance of a gigantic image was well adapted to represent successive kingdoms
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This image represented the kingdoms of the earth that should successively bear rule among the nations and have influence on the affairs of the Jewish church. The four monarchies were not represented by four distinct statues, but by one image, because they were all of one and the same spirit and genius

notes.short: The king finishes his threat but not his offer
notes.about: Nebuchadnezzar gives the three men another chance. He leaves unsaid what will follow if they bow to the statue, but spells out what they will suffer if they refuse: “you will be thrown at once into the blazing fiery furnace.”

figure.name: Aposiopesis
figure.words: worship the statue I have made
figure.means: what would follow if the men bowed, left unsaid, while the threat for refusing is spelled out

original.note: In Aramaic the first if-clause, “if you are ready,” runs on through the bowing down and has no then-clause; only the second, the threat, is finished.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Aposiopesis: the king was ready with his threat but careful to promise nothing. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the end of the first clause is left out as plain from the second, and compares Exodus 32:32. H. Deane (Ellicott's Commentary) says the word well is not in the Aramaic, where there is an aposiopesis, as in Exodus 32:32.
notes.limit: This translation renders the bowing down as a command, so the break shows only in the Aramaic. The writers differ on what is left unsaid: that the men would escape the furnace, or a promise the king took care not to make.

cites.quote: Here Nebuchadnezzar was ready with his threat of the punishment, but he was careful not to commit himself to any promise.

cites.quote: The conclusion to the first clause is omitted, because it is self-evident from the conclusion of the second, opposed passage: then ye will not be cast into the fiery furnace. Similar omissions are found in Exo 32:32 ; Luk 13:9 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Well. — The word is not in the Chaldee, where an aposiopesis is to be observed, as in Exo 32:32 .

notes.short: A great tree cut down pictures the proud king
notes.about: The king dreams of a great tree that shelters beasts and birds. A watcher from heaven orders it cut down, leaving the stump bound in the grass, and the words turn from the tree to a man given the mind of a beast. Daniel explains: “you, O king, are that tree!”

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: There was a tree in the midst of the land
figure.means: Nebuchadnezzar in his greatness: cut down for a time and left as a stump, he would lose his mind and his throne until he owned that the Most High rules

notes.evidence: Calvin says Nebuchadnezzar is meant under the figure of a tree, and that the whole is properly an allegory, a continued metaphor. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the tree with its roots is Nebuchadnezzar, the words passing from the type to the person it stands for. Albert Barnes calls the tree a striking emblem of a mighty monarch; Matthew Henry, a fit picture of him who reigned in Babylon.
notes.limit: The tree is a picture in the dream; what befell the king in verses 28 to 33 really happened. One writer also sees in the tree rulers in general, set by God to shelter those under them.

cites.quote: under the figure of a tree Nebuchadnezzar himself is intended, not because it fully represents the king’s office, but because God appointed the existence of governments in the world for this purpose—to be like trees on whose fruits all men feed ... nay, properly speaking, it is an allegory, since an allegory is only a continued metaphor.

cites.quote: the tree with its roots is Nebuchadnezzar, who shall as king be cut down, but shall as a man remain, and again shall grow into a king. ... the language passes from the type to the person represented by it.

notes.short: Four words on the wall, a riddle Daniel explains
notes.about: A hand writes four words on the palace wall, and the king’s wise men cannot read them or tell what they mean. Daniel, known to explain riddles, reads them and opens their sense: God has numbered Belshazzar’s reign, weighed him, and divided his kingdom. That very night the king was slain.

figure.name: Riddle
figure.means: God’s sentence on Belshazzar: his reign numbered and ended, the king weighed and found deficient, his kingdom divided and given to the Medes and Persians

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Daniel 5:25-28 under Ænigma: the handwriting is a riddle announcing Babylon’s fall, which Daniel interprets in verses 26-28. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch): the writing has the dark character of an oracle, each word holding a double sense the interpretation brings out. Matthew Henry calls it a riddle the wise men could not solve, so short we could make little of it unexplained.
notes.limit: The verses do not say why the wise men could not read the words, and the note does not guess.

cites.quote: The handwriting on the wall is given in the form of an Enigma, in which the immediate fall of Babylon was announced. ... These three words are interpreted by Daniel in verses 26-28, and the fulfilment of them follows in verses 30, 31.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Daniel now read the writing (Dan 5:25), and gave its interpretation (Dan 5:26-28). The writing bears the mysterious character of the oracle. ... In all the three words there lies a double sense, which is brought out in the interpretation.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Four beasts from the sea picture four kingdoms
notes.about: In a night vision Daniel sees four beasts come up out of the churning sea: a lion with eagle's wings, a bear, a leopard with four wings and four heads, and a dreadful fourth beast with iron teeth and ten horns, among which a little horn rises. Later he is told the beasts are four kings, or kingdoms.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: four great beasts came up out of the sea
figure.means: four kingdoms that would rise in turn, as Daniel is told in verses 17 and 23; the horns are kings who rise from the fourth

notes.evidence: Calvin says this is spoken allegorically, God painting a living image of each empire: the Chaldean a lion, the Persian a bear, the Macedonian a leopard, the fourth Rome. Albert Barnes: prophets often use animals to represent kingdoms. Clarke: the same meaning as the king's image, under other emblems. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch): beasts picture kingdoms, the lion answering to the golden head.
notes.limit: Daniel truly saw this vision; the beasts are what it showed him. The note keeps to the beasts and horns of verses 2 to 8, leaving aside the scene of the Ancient of Days that follows. Many read the four as Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome.

cites.quote: I have no doubt that in this vision the Prophet was shown the figure of the Roman Empire ... he formerly compared the Chaldean Empire to a lion, the Persian to a bear, and the Macedonian to a leopard. ... These things are spoken allegorically ... God wished to paint a kind of living image, in which he might show the peculiar characters of each government.

cites.quote: The design of mentioning them here, as coming up from, the sea, seems to have been to show that this succession of kingdoms sprang from the agitations and commotions among the nations represented by the heaving ocean. It is not uncommon for the prophets to make use of animals to represent or symbolize kingdoms and nations

notes.short: A ram and a goat picture two kingdoms
notes.about: In a vision Daniel sees a two-horned ram charging west, north and south, until a goat with one prominent horn tramples it. That horn is broken, four rise in its place, and a little horn grows great against the sanctuary. Gabriel explains that the ram represents Media and Persia, the goat Greece.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: a ram with two horns standing beside the canal
figure.means: the kings of Media and Persia, as Gabriel explains; the goat that tramples it is the king of Greece

notes.evidence: John Calvin says Persia and Media are here compared to a ram, one of the similitudes God set before His servant, both kingdoms under one emblem. Albert Barnes calls the ram a symbol that verse 20 explains. C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says ram and goat are emblems of kings, here Medo-Persia and the king of Javan, Greece. Adam Clarke says the ram pointed out that empire.
notes.limit: This is a vision, which the angel Gabriel explains from verse 19. Writers say more about whom the little horn stands for; the note keeps to what Gabriel names.

cites.quote: He now compares the empire of Persia and Media to a ram. It ought not to seem absurd that God proposed to his servant various similitude’s, because his duty was to teach a rude people in various ways ... Therefore, when the ram appeared to the Prophet, it represented both kingdoms under one emblem.

cites.quote: A ram which had two horns - There can be no error in explaining the design of this symbol, for in Dan 8:20 it is expressly said that it denoted the two kings of Media and Persia. The united power of the kingdom was denoted by the ram itself; the fact that there were two powers or kingdoms combined, by the two horns of the ram.
